extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, journalists, and media scholars interested in press-release pickup dynamics
extracted.subtask_description: A rubric for diagnosing when a press release functions as a 'pseudo-event' and for predicting how likely it is to be picked up by media, including operational features that increase pickup. Useful for PR producers assessing pickup probability and media scholars analyzing manufactured news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planned/Planted/Incited (not spontaneous)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release report something that was deliberately arranged for the purpose of being covered?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a meeting arranged so a press release can describe a 'summit'; an award created so the recipient can be named in a release. Diagnostic asks whether the event is spontaneous or manufactured to attract coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planted primarily to be reported / reproduced
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the existence of the event predominantly a function of its expected media coverage rather than serving an independent operational purpose?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on whether the primary raison d'être of the event is press attention (i.e., the event exists because it will be reported), as opposed to serving substantive organizational or public functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguous relation to underlying reality
rubrics_metrics.description: The pseudo-event has a thin substantive content and invites speculative interpretation — 'What does it mean?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the release's core claim lacks clear factual anchoring or substantive consequence, it is likely to provoke commentary and repetition rather than convey concrete information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-fulfilling prophecy
rubrics_metrics.description: The event becomes 'real' because it is reported; the release helps create the very condition it claims to describe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include market movements, trending topics, or perceived candidate 'momentum' that are manufactured or amplified by coverage prompted by the release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility / repeatability
rubrics_metrics.description: Pseudo-events are designed to be repeated (calendar-locked recurrence increases predictable pickup).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: annual rankings, monthly reports, 'year-in-review' releases. Recurrence makes editorial planning easier and increases likelihood of routine pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convenience for the reporting medium
rubrics_metrics.description: The pseudo-event is arranged for the convenience of the reporting or reproducing media; pickup correlates with how well the release respects media deadlines, formats, and crew availability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical fit with newsrooms — timing, length, format, and ease of covering (e.g., photo ops, local hooks) raise pickup probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-distributed text (news holdback/embargo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pseudo-events are often written up before they happen — releases issued in advance under embargo, with the event scripted to fit the release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing pre-written copy or embargoed materials that allow easy reuse increases the chance of reproduction and coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profitability for the medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Pseudo-events fill space at low cost; a release that reduces the marginal cost of column-inches or airtime is more likely to be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a release supplies ready-to-run content that saves editorial resources or fills scheduling gaps, it becomes economically attractive to outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mediocrity tolerance
rubrics_metrics.description: Pseudo-events are 'mediocre' — pitched neither too challenging nor too dull; releases aimed at the central tendency convert more reliably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoiding material that demands high cognitive effort or specialist expertise increases general pickup; aim for broadly comprehensible, middle-ground appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic enticement / spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Pseudo-events incorporate spectacle or dramatic elements (ribbon-cuttings, milestone charts, 'first' claims, celebrity sightings) to attract coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visuals, ceremonies, superlatives, and human-interest hooks increase the newsworthiness-as-seen-by-media and the chance of reproduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish pickup from public value (normative caveat)
rubrics_metrics.description: Boorstin's normative point: the pseudo-event is a symptom of cultural decay; a useful rubric separates 'high-pickup/low-public-value' from 'high-pickup/high-public-value' releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-pickup/low-public-value examples: arbitrary rankings, lightweight survey claims. High-pickup/high-public-value examples: releases that also convey substantive new information (peer-reviewed study results, earnings reports). The rubric predicts pickup but does not by itself justify the public value of the release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pickup-worthiness implication (predictive tradeoff)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pseudo-event characteristics predict pickup independent of substantive newsworthiness; optimizing a release along these characteristics increases pickup but may incur long-term credibility costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication for PR: designing releases to maximize reproducibility, convenience, pre-written copy, profitability, mediocrity tolerance, and spectacle will raise pickup rates, but repeated reliance on such tactics can produce audience cynicism and damage institutional credibility over time.
